guides.tandem.title: How does the tandem work?
guides.tandem.p1: The tandem slot goes to the last mutant placed in the incubator that has reached max experience. In other words, there are 2 priorities that decide which mutant becomes the tandem.
guides.tandem.li1Rest: — the tandem always holds one of your mutants with the highest Evo level; at max level, you also need to fill the XP bar all the way.
guides.tandem.li2Rest: — if Mutant A was placed in the incubator before Mutant B, then once both reach max level, it's Mutant B that becomes the tandem.
guides.tandem.p2: The order in which you level them up afterward doesn't matter. Even if you freeze Mutant A at level 1 and later decide to level it up and make it the tandem, once Mutant B reaches max level, Mutant A can never become the tandem again. The only fix is leveling up its Evo and keeping Mutant B at a lower level. But with all that hassle, it's usually easier to just breed a new mutant for the tandem.
guides.tandem.note: Important: you can't choose the tandem manually. Just like leveling up any other mutant to max — it only happens by placing a mutant in the incubator.
guides.pvpBug.title: PvP Bug (or Feature) Guide
guides.pvpBug.intro: No need to worry — you definitely won't get banned for this. You're not using any third-party software, just a small in-game trick that's been around for years.
guides.pvpBug.aboutP1: Toward the very end of the season you need to rack up at least 50 attacks (that's the requirement for landing in the top 1%. You can get away with 30 for 3%, but you'll likely end up with more anyway) and as good a PvP % as possible — a minimum of 10–11% (in practice, maybe 11–15%, but that's uncertain). You need to remember what % you had at the end of the season, right before the new one starts. It's best to check your final % in the morning before the new PvP starts, or at least during the night on the season's last day, since that's the number you'll need to go by.
guides.pvpBug.aboutP2: Say you ended up with 10%. As soon as the new season starts, you simply need to avoid entering PvP mode (don't even open the PvP section when choosing a battle mode, meaning don't even claim the reward for the previous PvP). You need to stay out for as many days (presumably) as the percentage you had in the previous PvP. Then you'll get all the rewards. Example: you had 10%. After the new season starts, don't enter PvP for 10 days — after that you can enter, and you'll be given all the rewards, including the mutant.
guides.pvpBug.howP1: The exact mechanism is unknown, but the theory is that when a new PvP season starts, players who claim their rewards from the previous season disappear from the old PvP's rankings, while people who didn't claim their rewards stay in it. That's how the ranking gradually thins out: most players at the top of the leaderboard claim their rewards in the first few days, and people from the bottom start climbing up that ranking and getting closer and closer to the top 1%. So the exact numbers here unfortunately can't be pinned down. But there's an approximate pattern — every day, your result from the previous season drops by ≈1%, until it reaches 1%, at which point you can claim the rewards.
guides.pvpBug.processLi1: You ended the previous season with 10%.
guides.pvpBug.processLi2: The new season starts — your previous result is still counted as 10%.
guides.pvpBug.processLi3: After roughly a couple of hours, enough players from the top of the leaderboard start PvP and claim their old-season rewards — now the result is counted as ≈9% (or even less).
guides.pvpBug.processLi4: On Tuesday — ≈8%, on Wednesday — ≈7%, and so on.
guides.pvpBug.processLi5: The following Tuesday arrives — your previous season's result is now ≈1%, and you can enter the mode and claim the rewards.
guides.pvpBug.note: A small tip — it's better to wait an extra 1–2 days as a buffer to be sure you'll get the rewards. If you don't need the mutant, you can wait until 3% — in that case you can shorten the wait by a couple of days. You can also aim not just for 10%, but for 9%, 8%, or even less — the bug will still work, it'll just shorten the wait.
guides.pvpBug.disclaimer: There may of course be inaccuracies here, but for now players go by the scheme described above.
guides.numbers.note: This section is based on reverse-engineering the game's binary — not guesses or estimates from observation.
guides.numbers.hp.title: HP growth per mutant level
guides.numbers.hp.p1: On each level up, a mutant gains +10% HP of its base HP (its HP at level 1).
guides.numbers.damage.title: Damage growth per mutant level
guides.numbers.damage.p1: Each level adds +10% of the mutant's attack at level 1 (not from the current attack, but specifically from the "base" value).
guides.numbers.damage.p2Intro: The game files originally define two sets of base stats for each mutant:
guides.numbers.damage.p2End: — the boosted base (kicks in starting at level 10 and 15 respectively).
guides.numbers.damage.p3: At level 10, the game doesn't just add a bonus to the current damage — it completely replaces the variable in the calculation formula: the old atk1 base is swapped for the boosted atk1p. After that, all accumulated per-level bonuses are recalculated as if the mutant had this new, higher attack since level 1. The same happens for the second attack (atk2), but at level 15.
guides.numbers.damage.formula1: Final damage (before level 10/15) = damage at level 1 × (level / 10 + 0.9)
guides.numbers.damage.formula2: Final damage (after level 10/15) = boosted damage at level 1 × (level / 10 + 0.9)
guides.numbers.damage.example: Example: at level 1 (atk1) a mutant has 200 attack — the game adds 10% (20 attack) per level, so at level 9 attack is 360. Without the base swap, at level 10 attack would become 380, but instead atk1 (200) is replaced with atk1p (300), and all accumulated bonuses (+90% from levels) are applied to the new base: 300 + 90% = 570. Every following level then adds 10% of atk1p (300).
guides.numbers.stars.title: Star bonuses to mutant stats
guides.numbers.stars.p1: Getting any star increases a mutant's stats (damage and HP) by the value that star gives: bronze ×1.1, silver ×1.3, gold ×1.75, platinum ×2.0.
guides.numbers.silver.title: Mutant silver income growth per level
guides.numbers.silver.p1: A mutant's base income is 42 units of silver per hour (silver/h). At higher levels, the base value is multiplied by the mutant's level. Some mutants have a different base income value.
guides.numbers.crit.title: Crit chance
guides.numbers.crit.p2: All crit chance bonuses (boosters + orbs) are added to it, and the whole sum is multiplied by that 5% — not added directly on top:
guides.numbers.crit.p3: Crit chance orbs boost the crit chance itself, not the damage it deals — the Russian in-game localization states otherwise, which is a translation error by the localizers.
guides.numbers.crit.boosterLine: The crit booster gives +50% of the received chance. The anti-crit booster gives −75% of the received chance.
guides.numbers.crit.table2SpheresBoosted: Crit chance with 2 orbs and boosters
guides.numbers.damageFormula.title: Damage formula
guides.numbers.damageFormula.p1: Base damage and an active attack buff/debuff are calculated as separate branches — each one goes through the crit and type modifier on its own, rather than the buff being added flatly on top of the final number:
guides.numbers.damageFormula.step1: base damage → crit (if it triggers, ×2) → type (±25% / ±50% from the table below)
guides.numbers.damageFormula.step2: separately: buff base → the same crit → the same type → the buff's % is taken from the result
guides.numbers.damageFormula.step3: total = result of step 1 + result of step 2
guides.numbers.damageFormula.example: Example: attack 10 000, crit triggers (×2), type +25%, attack buff +40%. Main branch: 10 000 → 20 000 → 25 000. Buff branch: 10 000 → 20 000 → 25 000 → 40% = 10 000. Total — 35 000, not 29 000 (a flat 25000+40% addition), and not a coincidental naive 35000 — the mechanic really is split into separate branches.
guides.numbers.typeTable.title: Damage reduction/bonus table
guides.numbers.typeTable.p1: The table shows how many percent of damage the attacker gains or loses against the defender's type.
guides.numbers.limits.title: Hidden number limits
guides.numbers.limits.p1: The game calculates some values as 32-bit numbers, and at certain limits this breaks.
guides.numbers.limits.hpP: With base HP above this threshold (without HP orbs), the value overflows and goes negative. HP orbs push the threshold even lower — the higher the % bonus, the earlier the bug hits.
guides.numbers.limits.speedP: The same class of bug as with HP. The threshold here doesn't depend on speed orbs.
guides.numbers.limits.goldP: When this value is crossed, the entire gold balance resets to 0 (it doesn't go negative — it's simply lost).
guides.numbers.limits.atkP: This is simply a value ceiling — once reached, attack stops growing further, but doesn't break or go negative.
guides.numbers.limits.silverP: Calculated as a 64-bit number — it's realistically impossible to hit this limit.
guides.numbers.limits.levelP: A regular stored value with no client-side calculations — there's nothing to overflow.
guides.numbers.bots.title: How bots think (PvE and PvP defense)
guides.numbers.bots.p1: PvE opponents and PvP defense use the exact same AI — there's no separate "defensive" algorithm. Every bot has a hidden "smartness" parameter (IQ), and it's decided anew on every turn:
guides.numbers.bots.step1: a random number from 0 to 99 is rolled
guides.numbers.bots.step2: number ≥ IQ — a random move: a random attack on a random living target, with no calculations at all
guides.numbers.bots.step3: number < IQ — a "smart" move: the bot genuinely simulates damage for every attack×target pair and picks the combination with the best fight outcome (if the attack is AOE, no further targets are tried)
guides.numbers.bots.p2: An important nuance: during this evaluation, a crit is mathematically impossible — the bot compares options using guaranteed non-crit damage. The actual crit roll happens once, at the moment of the real hit with the already-chosen move — using the same code that processes your own tap on the screen.
guides.numbers.bots.p3: The IQ value for a campaign fight isn't calculated — it's hand-hardcoded by the developers for each specific fight, growing alongside world progression:
guides.numbers.bots.tableIq: IQ of the chapter's early fights
guides.numbers.bots.p4: Within a single chapter, the IQ of the first ~6 "story" fights varies (see the table), while all other fights of that same chapter (replays/farming) always use 100.
guides.numbers.tandemHeal.title: Healing from an unused tandem
guides.numbers.tandemHeal.p1: A tandem you didn't use in a fight still heals your mutant — yes, tandems can heal.
guides.numbers.tandemHeal.formula: heal = tandem glory level × 100 ÷ 3 (or, equivalently, glory level ÷ 0,03)
guides.numbers.tandemHeal.p2: On a PvP defeat, the tandem doesn't heal — this heal only triggers on a win.
guides.numbers.skipCost.title: Cost of skipping an opponent in PvP
guides.numbers.skipCost.p1: Skipping an opponent in a PvP tournament costs silver, and the price depends not on your glory, but on the level of the opponent you're skipping:
guides.numbers.skipCost.p2Before: 250 silver per level is a constant from the game settings (
guides.numbers.skipCost.p2After: ). The higher the level of the shown opponent, the more expensive it is to skip them.
guides.intro.legendaries.p1: These mutants can result from breeding practically any mutants with matching genes (for example, Brawler + Brawler = Buck Maurice). The higher your Breeding Center level, the higher the chance of a legendary mutant appearing from a cross.
guides.intro.legendaries.p2: Of these mutants, only {name} is really worth your attention — definitely worth breeding. But if you're short on strong mutants early on, you can breed {starTrooper} and {dezinger}, or any mono-gene mutant from the list, since their stats are slightly inflated. Overall though, you'll usually find better options even among the secrets.
guides.intro.zodiac.p1: All mutants are tied to zodiac signs and appear on exactly the same dates as their real-world counterparts. We recommend getting them mainly for the collection and for bingo.
guides.intro.farmers.p1: A table of mutants with non-standard silver income. Most of them are event mutants that could be called near-worthless for farming, but we decided to include literally all of them here.
guides.intro.farmers.p2: Among the worthwhile new mutants, Dab and Zagam stand out, though the latter is way too expensive. The ratings are subjective but close to reality — they factor in income/hour, how easy (and comfortable) the mutant is to breed, the ability to farm outside lux zones, and how easy it is to obtain.
guides.intro.farmers.p3: You don't need to level up Midas, Bounty Hunter, or D.A.B. to a star for farming — at any star, they'll bring in the same amount of silver.
guides.intro.speedOrbs.p1: A table of the exact speed gain from level 3–5 speed orbs. When you give a mutant a speed orb, the % gain doesn't always match the 15%, 18%, and 20% printed on the orb itself — the actual gain for each specific base speed is shown in parentheses.
guides.intro.speedOrbs.p2: As you can see, the gain from the orb is almost always above nominal, especially at high speeds, where it can add up to 1–2 extra percent. It looks like each orb bonus was hand-tuned by the developers rather than calculated from a single formula — the speed with a given orb sometimes matches another mutant's base speed, or the same mutant's speed with a different orb level.
guides.intro.quests.p1: The game's main (non-event) quests with rewards — achievements, story quests, and system tasks. The game stores 5300+ missions, but most of them have neither a name nor a distinct reward — only the ones that actually look like a proper quest made it here: name → condition → reward.
guides.intro.divisions.p1: 7 campaign divisions (Alpha → Giga), each with 9 maps — the same 9 locations, but with rising enemy levels and rewards. The Evo-level and team-composition recommendations are our own estimate; the game itself gives no such hints.
guides.intro.ladders.p1: This lists practically every ladder that has ever existed in the game.
guides.intro.raids.p1: Raids are the hardest "ladders" in the game, but each one gives a unique mutant (that plays pretty well). Some raids don't have a proper in-game name — those names were invented by us based on the art's theme and are marked in italics.
guides.intro.specialOffers.p1: One-time offers that pop up when the player reaches a certain level (not to be confused with regular shop boxes — these are tied specifically to your level and shown only once).
